question: Tell me about a small improvement you made even though a bigger fix was supposedly just around the corner. Why did you act anyway?

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a small improvement you made even though a bigger fix was supposedly just around the corner. Why did you act anyway?

Our deployment script had a flaky step that failed 1 in 10 runs. The team said a full CI rewrite was coming in two months so no one touched it. I added a one-line retry with backoff and logged the failures. It cut our flaky rate to under 2% and saved me about two hours a week chasing logs.
What happened when the bigger rewrite landed?
The rewrite got delayed another quarter. My retry stayed in place and the logs helped the new CI team know what to keep.

junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Better than yesterday. The candidate owned a local pain point instead of waiting for the promised rewrite. The one-line retry delivered measurable reduction in flakiness and time spent. Even after the larger project slipped, the change remained useful and informed the replacement. This shows early ownership of incremental quality without overstepping scope. The main gap is that impact stayed within the candidate's own workflow rather than spreading further.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a small improvement you made even though a bigger fix was supposedly just around the corner. Why did you act anyway?

Two partner teams were duplicating customer-event validation logic. The org roadmap listed a shared service for Q3 so most people stopped maintaining their copies. I spent two days extracting a small shared library with the most common rules and got both teams to adopt it via a short RFC.
How did you get buy-in without the full service?
I showed each team their current duplication bugs and ran a one-week pilot that cut validation errors by 40%. The library stayed in use until the shared service replaced it six months later.

senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Better than yesterday. The candidate saw duplicated effort across teams and delivered a lightweight shared library instead of deferring to the distant service. The pilot provided concrete data that influenced two teams without formal authority. The interim solution reduced errors and remained in production for months. This demonstrates influence and incremental progress at a scope beyond a single team. The story could have included longer-term ownership transfer details.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a small improvement you made even though a bigger fix was supposedly just around the corner. Why did you act anyway?

Our quarterly planning process had inconsistent risk scoring that caused repeated re-prioritization fights. A full OKR and portfolio system was slated for next year so leaders kept using their own spreadsheets. I introduced a one-page risk rubric and required it for all Q2 proposals, then ran a retro after the quarter.
What changed at the org level?
Planning cycle time dropped 25% and leadership adopted the rubric as the interim standard. It shaped requirements for the new system and reduced re-work in two subsequent quarters.
